title: Exploratory analysis: look before you model
story:
You cannot read a million rows, so you compute summaries. The difficulty is that a summary is a lossy compression, and the losses were chosen before anyone saw what was being compressed.

The demonstration that settles this is small enough to check by hand. In 1973 Anscombe published four data sets of eleven observations each. They share a mean of x of 9 and a mean of y of 7.5, the same fitted regression line, the same regression and residual sums of squares, and therefore the same coefficient of determination of 0.67. Four numbers that a reader would take as a description of a relationship, identical across four situations that have almost nothing in common. One is a plausible linear relationship. One is a clean curve, where the relationship is obvious and not linear, which makes the correlation coefficient irrelevant. The others are dominated by single influential points.

Anscombe was explicit about the target. The article was written to counter an impression among statisticians that numerical calculations are exact, but graphs are rough — and the quartet's argument is that the exactness is real and beside the point, because the numbers are exact summaries of something they do not describe. Look at the four plots and the differences are obvious in a second. No amount of staring at the summaries would have revealed them, because the summaries are identical.

Tukey's book, published in 1977, gives the framing to carry: exploratory data analysis can never be the whole story, but nothing else can serve as the foundation stone, as the first step. Both halves matter. Exploration comes first because it tells you which summaries are meaningful, and it is not the whole story because it proves nothing — a pattern you found by looking is a hypothesis, and you found it in the same data you would like to test it on.

Which is the real cost of this activity and the reason it needs a discipline rather than enthusiasm. Looking has no completion criterion. There is always another view, another cut, another pair of columns, and a person examining enough views of enough columns will always find something. That is not a reason to skip it; it is a reason to write down what you expected before you look, to treat what you find as a hypothesis rather than a result, and to keep the exploring separate from the evaluating so the second is not contaminated by the first.

problem.name: Exploratory data analysis
problem.shape: There are too many rows to read, so the data reaches you as a handful of summary numbers chosen before anyone saw what they were summarising.
tell: a relationship is being described by a correlation or a fit statistic alone
a mean is quoted for a quantity with no reason to be symmetric
the analysis moved straight from loading the data to fitting a model
problem.move: Look before you summarise. Plot the distribution of each column you will use, the relationship you intend to model, and the residuals once you have fitted anything — and check whether a small number of points is carrying the result. Write down what you expected first, so that what you find can be recognised as a surprise rather than absorbed as a fact.
problem.invariant: A summary statistic is a lossy compression whose losses are decided in advance of seeing the data. Which summary is meaningful depends on the shape, and the shape is precisely what the summary discarded.
problem.breaks: Exploration has no completion criterion, and the same freedom that lets you notice the unexpected lets you find structure in noise — enough views of enough columns and something will always look like a pattern. So what exploration produces is a hypothesis, discovered in the data you would like to test it on, and it cannot also serve as the test.

cost.time: unbounded by nature, which is why it needs a stated stopping point rather than a feeling of completeness
cost.space: none; the plots are disposable and should be treated that way
cost.beats: going straight to a model, which produces exact numbers about a shape nobody has confirmed, and produces them with no indication that anything is wrong

worked.problem: Your coefficient of determination is 0.67. What does that tell you about the shape of the data?
worked.reasoning:
Nothing whatever about the shape. That is the entire point of the number and the entire danger of it.

Four data sets exist, of eleven points each, that share that value along with the same mean of x, the same mean of y, the same fitted line, and the same regression and residual sums of squares. One is a straightforward linear relationship. One is a clean curve, where the relationship is obvious and not linear, so the correlation coefficient is not merely weak but irrelevant. In the others a single influential point is doing the work — remove it and the fitted line goes somewhere else entirely.

So the honest reading is that the number tells you how much of the variance the fitted line accounts for, under the assumption that a line is the right thing to fit. It cannot tell you whether that assumption holds, because it is computed after the assumption has been made. A high value on a curved relationship means the line is a decent approximation to a shape it is the wrong family for, and a value driven by one point tells you about that point rather than about the relationship.

What I would want instead, before quoting any such figure, is the scatter plot; residuals plotted against the fitted values, where curvature and changing spread announce themselves; and some check of influence, since the concern is a small number of points rather than the bulk.

The general lesson is that every summary statistic is a lossy compression with the losses fixed in advance. It is not that summaries are bad — they are how you handle a million rows — but that which summary is meaningful depends on the shape, and the shape is the thing the summary discarded. Anscombe's point was that the calculations are perfectly exact and that their exactness is beside the question, and he wrote the quartet specifically to counter the belief that numerical calculations are exact while graphs are rough.

problem.practice: Take the four classic data sets and compute their summaries yourself, confirming that they agree. Then plot them. After that, take a relationship from your own work that you have only ever described with a fit statistic, plot it, and plot the residuals against the fitted values.

beats.broke: You cannot read a million rows, so you compute summaries — and a summary is a lossy compression whose losses were chosen before anyone saw what was being compressed.
beats.fix: Look at the shape first, because the shape decides whether a given summary means anything. Four data sets of eleven points can share their means, their fitted line, their sums of squares and their fit statistic while describing entirely unrelated situations.
beats.cost: Looking has no completion criterion and actively invites finding structure in noise, so what it yields is a hypothesis discovered in the very data you would like to test it on — the foundation stone, as the 1977 formulation has it, and never the whole story.

interview.q: Your coefficient of determination is 0.67. What does that tell you about the shape of the data?
interview.trap: Reading it as a description of the relationship — moderately strong, roughly linear. It is computed after a line has been assumed and therefore cannot be evidence that a line was the right thing to assume.
interview.answer:
Nothing about the shape at all, which is both the point of the number and the danger of it.

There are four well-known data sets of eleven points each that share that value, along with the same mean of x, the same mean of y, the same fitted line and the same regression and residual sums of squares. One is a straightforward linear relationship. One is a clean curve, where the relationship is obvious but not linear, so the correlation coefficient is irrelevant rather than merely weak. In the remaining two a single influential point is doing the work, and removing it sends the fitted line somewhere else entirely.

What the number actually reports is how much of the variance the fitted line accounts for, on the assumption that a line is the right thing to fit. It is computed after that assumption has been made, so it cannot be evidence for it. A high value on a curved relationship just means a line approximates a shape from the wrong family reasonably well, and a value driven by one point is a fact about that point.

Before quoting such a figure I would want three things: the scatter plot; residuals against fitted values, where curvature and changing spread reveal themselves immediately; and an influence check, because the failure mode is a handful of points rather than the bulk.

The general form of the answer is that every summary is a lossy compression whose losses were fixed before anyone saw the data. Summaries are not the problem — they are how a million rows become tractable — but which summary is meaningful depends on the shape, and the shape is exactly what the summary threw away.

blueprint:
A SUMMARY IS LOSSY COMPRESSION
WITH THE LOSSES CHOSEN IN ADVANCE

   1973, four sets of 11 points:

      same mean x (9), same mean y (7.5),
      same fitted line, same sums of squares,
      same coefficient of determination (0.67)

      -> a linear relationship
      -> a clean curve
      -> a line plus an outlier
      -> one point doing all the work

   identical numbers. unrelated situations.

WHY NO AMOUNT OF STARING HELPS

   the summaries are the SAME.
   the information that distinguishes them was
   discarded at the moment of summarising.

   the plots differ in ONE SECOND.

THE ORDER OF OPERATIONS

   look  ->  choose summaries  ->  quote them

   not:  quote  ->  look if something seems odd

WHAT EXPLORATION IS AND IS NOT

   IS      the foundation stone. the first step.
           it tells you which summaries mean
           anything.

   IS NOT  the whole story. a pattern you found
           by looking is a HYPOTHESIS -- and you
           found it in the data you would like
           to test it on.

THE DISCIPLINE, BECAUSE LOOKING NEVER FINISHES

   write down what you expect BEFORE you look
   treat findings as hypotheses, not results
   keep exploring separate from evaluating
takeaway: Four data sets of eleven points can agree on every summary a report would quote and disagree completely about what is happening — so the summary tells you nothing about the shape, and the shape is what decides whether the summary means anything.
